# Log Store

## Overview

The store keeps the winter fuel dry and off the ground, which is the whole job. It backs onto the north wall of the garage, where the wall blocks the prevailing weather and gives me a solid face to fix the frame against. The wind that gets through the open front is the whole point of the design: it moves air across the split faces and carries the moisture off, slowly, over months. Without that draught the pile would sit damp, grow a beard of mould and burn badly. It took a weekend to build from rough sawn board and a sheet of corrugated tin, and it has stood for six years without a repair beyond a new floor board. The two bays together hold enough to see me through a winter and leave a bay to fill. Before it went up I kept the fuel under a tarpaulin against the shed, and the bottom layer came out white with mould every time. The site gets sun from mid morning, which helps the front face dry after a wet spell. What follows is how I built it, how I look after it, and what I have learned about filling it.

## Building

The whole thing is two bays, each about 2 m wide and 1.2 m deep, for roughly four cubic metres of stacked fuel when they are full. I set the bays side by side against the garage wall, sharing a centre post, which gives me one bay to draw from and one to fill. The floor is a slatted deck raised on 100 mm bearers, so the bottom layer of splits sits clear of the ground and the air moves under the pile as well as through it. The bearers are treated, set on flat pads of slate so they do not sink into the soil. A solid floor here would rot from the underside within two winters, and it would take the bottom row of fuel with it.

The frame is rough sawn timber, four uprights at the corners and one in the middle, braced with a diagonal on each end. The roof is a single sheet of corrugated tin, sloped back to front so rain runs off the open face rather than into the bays. I laid a strip of flashing where the tin meets the garage wall and turned the edge up against the render. The front is left completely open, no doors and no slats, because anything across the face blocks the draught that does the drying. The shelter is the roof, and the open front is the vent.

Along the back I left an air gap. The bays stand about 50 mm clear of the garage wall, held off by short blocks on the top and bottom rails, so air can move up behind the stack and out under the roof edge. Without that gap the wall side of the pile sweats against the render, and I have seen that happen in a neighbour's open-sided shelter: the back row went black while the front was fine. The gap is invisible from the path and it is the difference between a store that dries fuel and one that holds water against it.

## Maintenance

The floor gets swept out once a year, in autumn, before the new fill goes in. I take the last of the old fuel out of the bay, pull the boards, brush them and stack them back, and rake out the dust and crumbs that have dropped between the slats. The boards take the weather at the front edge and one of them splits after a few winters, so I keep a spare cut to length in the rafters and swap it when the crack opens. The sweepings go on the path, and a little soot and ash shake out of the sweepings when I tip them on the path, which is why I do not put them on the beds. I check the tin roof for lifted nails each autumn and tap the flashing back down where the wind has worked it loose. I also clear the leaves that gather in the air gap along the back, since a winter of wet leaves packed against the render is exactly what the gap is meant to prevent. The bearer blocks get a look while I am down there, and I slide a slate back under any that has shifted. The white plastic sheet I keep over the top of a part-filled bay in winter comes off in March. That is the whole of the maintenance, and it takes an hour.

## Notes

Everything in the stack sits for two winters before it burns. The first winter dries it from the wet it was cut at, and the second brings the middle of the splits down to proper burning moisture, which for me is when the meter reads 18% on a freshly split face. I test a few pieces from the middle of the pile before I start drawing from a bay, because the outside of a split can read low while the core is still wet. The top bay is the newer one and the lower bay is the one I draw from, so the fill always moves through in order and nothing gets left at the back for years. I stack the splits bark up where I can, loosely, with the ends facing the open front, and I never fill a bay right to the roof, since the gap above lets the air turn over the top of the pile. When the lower bay runs low in February I refill it from the upper one and start filling the top again in spring, which keeps the two-winter cycle turning without me having to think about it much. I check a split from the middle with the meter before I carry a barrow in, and any piece reading 25% or more goes back into the upper bay for another year. The ends go pale and checked long before the middle is dry, so the ends are no guide to what is inside. A handful of splits I bring indoors for a day before they go on the stove, which takes the last of the chill off them and makes the fire catch quicker. The bays are wide enough to take a barrow a load at a time, and I wheel it straight in rather than throwing the splits over the front rail.
